title: Halloween: Resurrection
full_review:
Six college students agree to spend Halloween night in the childhood home of serial killer Michael Myers in the dopey horror thriller "Halloween: Resurrection" (Dimension).

The eighth installment of John Carpenter's worn-out Halloween series, which was first introduced in 1978, follows a predictably murderous pattern without an ounce of credibility. The audience's interest is only mildly aroused to figure out which of the six co-eds will be picked off first by the homicidal maniac Myers (portrayed by stuntman/actor Brad Loree). The crew of three gals and three guys win a contest to spend the night in his creepy home to launch a live Internet chat show, which most of them hope will blast-off their broadcasting/Hollywood careers. Naturally Myers is alive and well, still thirsty for blood and living cozily in a hidden room under the house. And wouldn't you know it, the students' arrival leads to another killing spree by the madman.

Not a second of this 85-minute film is original. Even the decapitations and stabbings are played out. Several scenes have Myers, attired in his familiar ghostly white mask and drab workman's jumpsuit, skulking about, chef's knife in the air with the tip soaked in the blood of his last victim. It's laughable - no longer frightening - to see Myers walking calmly behind his prey while he or she scurries up stairs or high-tails it down a corridor. All the while the audience knows he will catch up to them despite the speed disparity. The idiotic plot is completely devoid of tension or suspense, telegraphing every twist and turn in each scene.

Hip hop star Busta Rhymes stars as the mastermind behind the Internet show with his side kick Tyra Banks working the control room. Her tiny role consists mainly of looking pretty, making cappuccino and allowing the camera to follow her curvy body as she prances around to a favorite tune. Rhymes improvises most of his lines, letting loose with expletives when coherent dialogue would have been much better. Of the six students, there is the obligatory smart and sensitive girl, Sara (Bianca Kajlich), who seems like the one most likely to survive. Jamie Lee Curtis returns as Laurie Strode, Myers' sister who is in a mental institution. Her eerie voice-over during the opening scene falsely indicates that the movie may have something to offer. It doesn't.

The film alternates between the grainy digital visuals representing what the Internet audience is seeing and the overcast images of the rest of film that aspire to be spooky, but instead just look muddy.

"Halloween: Resurrection" is only scary in how dim-witted its creators are in thinking that another stale installment that was slapped together in the most haphazard of ways could possibly pass horror-film muster.

Because of intermittent stylized violence, mild sexual innuendo, fleeting nudity and drug use and recurring rough language with brief profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.(
2002
)
